entries.label: We look for evidence of exceptional ability. Please provide us with 3-4 examples highlighting your exceptional ability, using quantitative metrics to display the impact on a product/project related to the requirements of the position you are applying for. Each bullet should be very concise— no longer than 3-4 sentences each and should capture the problem, solution, and result. We recommend starting with an action word (designed, led, built, promoted, launched, created, etc.) and be sure to include technical detail. This is your moment to WOW us! NOTE: Answering this question fully is the most important part of our interview process. First example:
entries.value: Built and shipped ClarityAtlas, an iOS health product, end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with a Supabase backend, as co-founder and technical lead of Open Health Intelligence. The core technical problem was estimating sleep without a wearable, so I built a passive sleep-estimation system that infers sleep from phone-interaction and motion signals, using HealthKit and Core Motion inputs like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns, plus backend services for behavioral comparison including a "Sleep Twins" matching system based on standardized features and weighted distance. I shipped it into a live pilot at Johns Hopkins with 30+ users, and the project was selected for the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps and drew a non-binding investment indication of roughly $75,000 for about 7 to 8% equity. It taught me how noisy body-signal inference behaves once real users depend on it daily, which is the part I would want to carry into decoding work on BCI Applications.

entries.label: Second example:
entries.value: A second example is ClarityAtlas, an iOS health product I co-founded Open Health Intelligence to build and served as technical lead on. I built it end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with a Supabase backend. The hardest technical piece was estimating sleep without a wearable, so I built a passive sleep-estimation system from phone-interaction and motion signals, using HealthKit and Core Motion inputs such as step count, gait speed, and movement patterns. That meant inferring a physiological state from noisy, indirect sensor streams rather than measuring it directly. I also built backend services for behavioral comparison, including a "Sleep Twins" matching system using standardized behavioral features and weighted distance. We shipped it into a live pilot at Johns Hopkins with 30 or more users, and the project was selected for the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps. What I took from it is that shipping to real users exposes failure modes no local test does, which is the part I would want to carry into work on interfaces people actually depend on daily.
